Isn't October just so beautiful? 🥰 Along with the stunning scenery, it also brings with it some new gardening tasks to finish up. With some milder weather in the forecast for the next few days, maybe you can spend some time in the gardens! 🏡

🍂 October Garden Checklist 🍂
🔘 Plant spring flowering bulbs.
🔘 Divide spring/summer blooming perennials
🔘 Transplant shrubs or young trees to new locations.
🔘 Cut diseased areas out of perennials. Do not compost.
🔘 Remove all vegetable plants and fallen fruit.
🔘 Remove dead annuals from the garden, after a frost.
🔘 Cut back perennial foliage (like hostas) if desired.
🔘 Leave flowers with seeds (like coneflowers) for the birds.
🔘 Continue watering trees and shrubs as needed until the ground freezes.
🔘 Sharpen lawn mower blade and pruners.
🔘 Dig up tender bulbs such as dahlia, canna and gladiola. Store in a cool, dry and dark space.
🔘 Prep areas to sow seeds that require cold stratification (like poppies or milkweed).

🌿 October in the Garden 🌿

October in the garden — a time to harvest, plant, and prepare for the seasons ahead. 

Here’s what we’re working on this month:

🍁 Harvest: Gather your fall harvest such as Maypop passionfruit, hibiscus, ginger or other roots that aren’t cold hardy, squash, pumpkins, and hawthorn berries. These can be stored, dried, or turned into syrups and teas to last through winter.

🌱 Plant: Get garlic and spring bulbs in the ground before frost. Sow cool-weather greens like kale, cabbage, chard, and broccoli — they’ll thrive as temperatures drop. Create weather protecion such as row cover for them.

🪴 Protect: Pot up tender herbs and non-cold-hardy plants to overwinter indoors. Compost fallen leaves and garden scraps to feed next season’s soil.

🐝 Support Wildlife: Leave some leaf litter and seed heads for beneficial insects and birds. Set up a feeder or brush pile for shelter during colder months.

🌾 Save: Collect and label seeds from favorite flowers and herbs for next year’s planting.

Ready, set, winterize! ❄️ This weekend is a fantastic time to begin prepping your garden for the months ahead!

Here are 5 tips to ensure your garden beds are winter-ready:

🌱 Trim & Tidy: Prune away dead or overgrown branches to encourage healthy growth and prevent winter damage.

🌱 Harvest & Hibernate: Gather the last of your garden harvest before the frost arrives.

🌱 Hydrate: Give your plants deep water before the frost sets in to keep them well-hydrated during the coming weeks. 

🌱 A Layer of Comfort: Provide your plants with a cozy blanket by adding 1-2 inches of processed compost, mushroom manure, or sea soil to the top of your garden beds. Cover with mulch for extra protection.

🌱 Cozy Containers: If you have potted plants, move them to sheltered areas or wrap them in burlap to shield them against the winter winds.

Turn Fall Leaves Into Free Mulch! 

Instead of bagging up leaves this fall, put them to work in your landscape! Leaves are a free, natural resource that can improve soil, suppress weeds, and feed your plants.

Two easy ways to use them:
1. Shred with a mower: Chop dry leaves right on your lawn or collect them to mulch garden beds. Shredded leaves break down quickly, adding nutrients and organic matter to the soil.
2. Pile them up: Whole leaves will slowly decompose into leaf mold, a rich soil amendment that improves structure and moisture retention.

Tuesday Tips! 🌷🪻 Ready to secure a gorgeous spring garden in Minnesota? The best time to plant your spring-blooming bulbs is NOW—typically from late September through October.

Here's a quick guide for getting those beautiful blooms ready for next spring:

⏰ The Minnesota Timing Window
When: Mid-September to mid-October is prime time. Planting now gives your bulbs several weeks to establish strong roots before the ground freezes solid.
The Late Exception: You can often plant Tulips as late as you can still dig a hole, even into early November, but earlier is always better for most bulbs.

💡 Quick Planting Tips for MN Success
Check the Bulb: Only plant bulbs that are firm and heavy for their size—toss any that are soft or moldy.
Plant Deep: A general rule is to plant the bulb about 3 times its height deep. Large bulbs (Daffodils, Tulips) go 6-8 inches deep; smaller bulbs (Crocus, Muscari) go 3-4 inches deep.
Pointy Side Up: Place the bulb with the pointed tip facing up and the flatter, root-end down.
Group for Impact: Skip the straight lines! Plant bulbs in clusters of 5, 7, 9, or more for a lush, natural look.
Water & Mulch: Water thoroughly after planting. After the ground freezes, cover the area with a 2-3 inch layer of mulch (like straw or leaves) for extra insulation.

🍂 Fall Garden Swaps: Make the Most of Your Space! 🌱

As summer crops finish up, it’s a great time to replant with cool-season veggies that thrive in the months ahead. Here’s a simple guide to what you can plant next and why these swaps work so well:

🔁 Tomatoes ➡️ Peas
Peas can climb the same trellis and naturally add nitrogen back to the soil

🔁 Cucumbers ➡️ Spinach or Kale
These leafy greens love cooler weather and grow fast in cucumber-sized spaces

🔁 Zucchini ➡️ Carrots or Radishes
The loose, fertile soil left by zucchini is ideal for root crops to develop

🔁 Beans ➡️ Broccoli
Broccoli benefits from the nitrogen-rich soil beans leave behind

🔁 Peppers ➡️ Garlic or Onions
Alliums help discourage pests that may be lingering after peppers

🔁 Melons ➡️ Mustard Greens
Mustard acts as a natural soil cleanser, helping reduce pests and disease

🔁 Basil ➡️ Cilantro or Parsley
These herbs prefer cooler temps and are great for fall cooking

Planning your next planting with crop rotation in mind can improve your harvest and support healthier soil for seasons to come! 🌿

The Role of Organic Fertilizers in Sustainable Agriculture

In the face of growing environmental challenges and the need for sustainable food production, organic fertilizers have emerged as a key player in promoting eco-friendly agricultural practices. 

One of the most effective ways to achieve sustainable agriculture is through the use of organic fertilizers.

In today’s post, we will explore the role of organic fertilizers in sustainable agriculture, their benefits, and why they are the future of farming in Nigeria and beyond.

What are Organic Fertilizers?

Organic fertilizers are naturally derived from plant, animal, or mineral sources. They include compost, manure, bio-slurry, bone meal, and green manure. 

Unlike chemical fertilizers, organic fertilizers improve soil fertility without harmful side effects, making them essential for sustainable farming systems.

Why is Sustainable Agriculture Important?

Sustainable agriculture focuses on meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to produce food. 

It promotes practices that maintain soil health, conserve water, and reduce pollution – all while increasing productivity.

With the increasing threat of climate change, soil degradation, and water pollution, the need for sustainable farming methods has never been greater.

Compost is organic material that can be added to soil to help plants grow. Food scraps and garden waste together currently make up more than 28% of what we throw away, and should be composted instead. Making compost keeps these materials out of landfills where they take up space and release methane, a potent greenhouse gas. 

Composting is very beneficial as it :

Enriches soil, helping retain moisture and suppress plant diseases and pests.

Reduces the need for chemical fertilizers.

Encourages the production of beneficial bacteria and fungi that break down organic matter to create humus, a rich nutrient-filled material.

Reduces methane emissions from landfills and lowers your carbon footprint.
 
Composting organisms require 4 conditions to create compost:

∆ Carbon that comes from brown organic matter like dried leaves and grasses 
sawdust, paper,twigs etc

∆  Nitrogen that comes from fruit and vegetable waste, tea, coffee grounds

∆ Oxygen which comes from proper aeration

∆  And moisture in right amounts

5 easy steps to compost your kitchen & garden waste :

1. Separate your edible kitchen waste (vegetable peels, fruit peels, and dry organic matter (dried leaves, sawdust),twigs in a small container

2. Take a large earthen pot  and drill holes around the container for proper aeration

4. Fill the bottom with a layer of soil and
 start adding food waste in layers alternating wet waste (food scraps, vegetable and fruit peels) with dry waste (straw, sawdust, dried leaves), and add some organic fertilizer or compost from the previous batch to speed up the decomposition process and cover this container with a wooden plank to keep it moist.

5.After every few days, give the pile a quick turn to provide aeration.
Within 30-45 days your pile will be ready to be used, with time and a little patience you can make your own pot of black gold for your green friends..🙂

Comfrey tea DIY organic fertilizer!

Comfrey is an amazing multipurpose plant with many benefits. It has a deep tap root that reaches down in the earth and "mines" nutrients from the ground, bringing them up to the surface through it's leaves. When the leaves decompose, the nutrients then become available for the surrounding plants, making it a great companion plant. It also attracts beneficial pollinators, providing essential food for bees. Not to mention, it's also medicinal! Also known as "knit bone," a comfrey compress helps speed recover after a sprain or broken bone. 
How to make comfrey tea fertilizer:

1. Trim your comfrey plant, leaving the small new growth.

2. Bend the stems and "wring" them (leaves and all) to break up the fibers.

3. Place the plant in a mesh bag (I use some landscaping fabric sewn into a bag). Place inside a bucket.

4. Fill bucket with water, close lid, and let ferment for about 2 weeks in a spot away from the house (comfrey tea can get kinda stinky). 5. When ready, wring out all the water from the bag. 
6. Add one cup of tea to every gallon of water when fertilizing plants. 
7. Discard the partially decomposed material in the compost.

How do you know when the stems are dead? It depends on which variety you have and where you live but if they are brown, with no growth on them and/or the buds aren’t turning green by mid-May, I would cut them down to the ground and cross your fingers you have a hybrid because then you will likely get flowers off the new growth (Endless Summer is an example but some people refer to these as “Endless Bummers”😂)

It’s often too cold in New England and other areas in the US for these but breeders create new varieties all the time.
Yes, these are beautiful when they work but they aren’t reliable so I recommend you plant something that will deliver. I am a huge fan of oakleaf hydrangeas, panicles (like Limelight and other varieties), and wild arborescens (cultivated versions include Annabelle and Incrediball). These are all reliable bloomers and are less finisky than the bigleafs. Serratas are also solid.

When you get right down to it I am a pretty lazy gardener. I like to cut corners and save my energy and time for something fun like expanding new areas; tasks that result in a good return on my investment, like deadheading to get more flowers; drudgery like weeding; watering plants to help them get established or to prevent established plants from dying; and pruning, which is a task that is needed and which I love but which can still feel like a chore. 

Being lazy can also have several wonderful additional benefits: 1. It’s good for the soil because everything breaks down. 2. It acts as mulch so it helps to minimize weeds and retain moisture, as well as regulating soil temperature. 3. It provides habitat for insects and other creatures over the winter, which results in more available food in the spring. 4. And it can provide food over the winter for birds. 

Why doesn’t everyone do this? They don’t know, they don’t like a “messy” garden, or they have restrictions on how a garden looks. If you are in the last two categories, modify this slightly to make it work for you. (And them.)

🎆JULY Planting + Planning🎆
July is undoubtedly one of our hottest months in the southeast. With that, we have to be careful of a few things - planting, watering, and preserving the plants we already have. The planting list is very limited, as you can see, unless you are sowing seeds for fall and winter. The biggest part of the summer is preserving - fighting off those pests (as needed), making sure your plants get enough water, and providing them with additional protection (mulch) and nutrients (fertilizer/ compost).

How-to: plant out your tomato seedlings. 🍅 Growing great tomatoes is a skill available to just about anyone. But there are a few tricks to getting things right, including during the planting out stage. ⁠
⁠
First up, before you get your hands dirty, it's best to plan how you're going to plant your toms - in a block or in a row? How far apart? Will you need a trellis? Then you'll need to prepare your soil and have a think about mulch...⁠
⁠
You can find details on all these steps at the 🔗 link in our bio 🔗 today.⁠
⁠
Alrighty - once you're ready to plant your seedlings out, here's how to do it:⁠
⁠
🍅 Use a garden trowel to make a hole in the mulch that’s about 15 cm (6 inches) wide and one and a half times as deep as the pot. Repeat for each tomato plant, spacing them according to your planting plan.⁠
⁠
🍅 Gently turn the pot upside down, with the seedling between your fingers and your hand flat against the surface of the soil, and remove from the pot.⁠
⁠
🍅 Plant your tomatoes deep, covering at least the bottom sets of leaves if you can - preferably more! These nodes will magically transform into roots as the tomato senses they have been buried. The more roots for your tomato plant, the better access it has to nutrients and water.⁠
⁠
🍅 Press the garden bed soil in around your little seedling and water it in with some diluted liquid fertiliser – we use home-made seaweed fertilizer.⁠
⁠
🍅 Make sure you leave some space in the mulch around the seedling to allow for good airflow… and your tomatoes are in!⁠
⁠
Happy tomato planting, southern folk - may it be a season of plentiful tomatoes, with a pantry full of sauces and preserves.⁠

5. Transplant and Divide: Move plants that are not sited properly for best performance. Separate large clumps to replant and share with your gardening friends and neighbors.(Be careful not to share invasive plants).

Charlies Winter Pruning Tips:🍂
“I like to give my deciduous trees and shrubs a really good prune as you can see the shape of the plant and pruning them is much easier without the weight of leaves. I was once told, if you can make a tree look good naked then come Spring, it can only look amazing.
Start by removing any crossing or rubbing branches. These cause wounds on the tree and infections can easily get into the plant so early removal is a bonus.
I then prune to shape, looking at where the plant will shoot from and prune according to the new growth it will put on come springtime.
When pruning larger branches, use a three-step cut system to prevent the bark from ripping. The first cut should be from the underside of the branch upwards and only about a third of the way through the branch.
The second cut from the top down, starting further out from the trunk than the first cut so when the branch breaks off it only rips to the point of the first cut. The third cut is the last cut closest to the trunk to tidy things up.”
Charlie Albone Richgro Brand Ambassador
